claim: A molecular model of the E. coli F-ATP synthase was generated using cryo-electron microscopy.
source: A molecular model that provides a framework for interpreting the wealth of functional information obtained on the E. coli F-ATP synthase has been generated using cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that cryo-EM was used to generate the molecular model.

claim: Three different rotational states of the E. coli F-ATP synthase were observed.
source: Three different states that relate to rotation of the enzyme were observed, with the central stalk's ε subunit in an extended autoinhibitory conformation in all three states.
evidence: The abstract and results describe three distinct states observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: The central stalk's ε subunit is in an extended autoinhibitory conformation in all three observed states.
source: Three different states that relate to rotation of the enzyme were observed, with the central stalk's ε subunit in an extended autoinhibitory conformation in all three states.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The Fo motor comprises seven transmembrane helices and a decameric c-ring.
source: The Fo motor comprises of seven transmembrane helices and a decameric c-ring and invaginations on either side of the membrane indicate the entry and exit channels for protons.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the composition of the Fo motor based on the cryo-EM structures.

claim: Invaginations on either side of the membrane indicate the entry and exit channels for protons.
source: The Fo motor comprises of seven transmembrane helices and a decameric c-ring and invaginations on either side of the membrane indicate the entry and exit channels for protons.
evidence: The abstract states that invaginations observed in the structure indicate proton channels.

claim: The proton translocating subunit contains near parallel helices inclined by ~30° to the membrane.
source: The proton translocating subunit contains near parallel helices inclined by ~30° to the membrane, a feature now synonymous with rotary ATPases.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this structural feature observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: Near parallel helices inclined by ~30° to the membrane is a feature synonymous with rotary ATPases.
source: The proton translocating subunit contains near parallel helices inclined by ~30° to the membrane, a feature now synonymous with rotary ATPases.
evidence: The abstract states this is a known feature of rotary ATPases.

claim: The peripheral stalk is resolved over its entire length of the complex for the first time in this rotary ATPase subtype.
source: For the first time in this rotary ATPase subtype, the peripheral stalk is resolved over its entire length of the complex, revealing the F1 attachment points and a coiled-coil that bifurcates toward the membrane with its helices separating to embrace subunit a from two sides.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this is the first time the entire peripheral stalk has been resolved for this ATPase subtype.

claim: The peripheral stalk contains a coiled-coil that bifurcates toward the membrane with its helices separating to embrace subunit a from two sides.
source: For the first time in this rotary ATPase subtype, the peripheral stalk is resolved over its entire length of the complex, revealing the F1 attachment points and a coiled-coil that bifurcates toward the membrane with its helices separating to embrace subunit a from two sides.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this structural feature observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: ATP synthase couples ion flow across membranes with the addition of inorganic phosphate to ADP thereby generating ATP.
source: This molecular generator couples ion flow across membranes with the addition of inorganic phosphate (Pi) to ADP thereby generating ATP (Iino and Noji, 2013; Stewart et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction states this mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: E. coli has only one type of rotary ATPase, referred to as F-type ATPase.
source: Most bacteria, including Escherichia coli have only one type of rotary ATPase, referred to as F-type ATPase.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this fact about E. coli.

claim: F-type ATPase is based on two reversible motors, termed F1 and Fo, connected by central and peripheral stalks.
source: Like the analogous complexes in other kingdoms, it is based on two reversible motors, termed F1 and Fo (Negrin et al., 1980), connected by central and peripheral stalks (Wilkens and Capaldi, 1998a) (Figure 1).
evidence: The introduction describes the basic architecture with supporting citations.

claim: The Fo motor spans the membrane converting the potential energy of the proton motive force into rotation of the central stalk.
source: The Fo motor spans the membrane converting the potential energy of the proton motive force (pmf) into rotation of the central stalk that in turn drives conformational changes in the F1 catalytic sites.
evidence: The introduction describes the function of the Fo motor.

claim: The c-ring in E. coli F-ATPase has decameric stoichiometry.
source: Subunit c assembles into a ring, thought, in E. coli, to have decameric stoichiometry (Jiang et al., 2001; Ballhausen et al., 2009; Düser et al., 2009; Ishmukhametov et al., 2010), whereas subunits a and b associate to form a helical bundle adjacent to this ring.
evidence: The introduction states this with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: A four-helix bundle of subunit a, inclined by 20–30˚ to the membrane plane, forms a crucial structural component.
source: All structures confirm that a four-helix bundle of subunit a, inclined by 20–30˚ to the membrane plane, forms a crucial structural component.
evidence: The introduction states this structural feature is confirmed by multiple structures.

claim: Protons from the bacterial periplasm access a conserved negatively charged carboxylate in subunit c (Asp61 in E. coli) through an aqueous half channel at the subunit a/c interface.
source: In this mechanism, protons from the bacterial periplasm access a conserved negatively charged carboxylate in subunit c (Asp61 in E. coli [Hoppe et al., 1982]) through an aqueous half channel at the subunit a/c interface (Steed and Fillingame, 2008).
evidence: The introduction describes the proton translocation mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: Neutralizing the conserved carboxylate in subunit c enables the c-ring to rotate within the hydrophobic membrane.
source: Neutralizing this carboxylate enables the c-ring to rotate within the hydrophobic membrane and to access a second aqueous half channel that opens to the cytoplasm into which the protons are released (Pogoryelov et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction describes the mechanism with a supporting citation.

claim: A conserved arginine residue in helix-4 of subunit a (Arg210 in E. coli) prevents the c-ring rotating in the opposite direction and short-circuiting of the system.
source: A conserved arginine residue in helix-4 of subunit a (Arg210 in E. coli) prevents the c-ring rotating in the opposite direction and short-circuiting of the system (Lightowlers et al., 1987; Cain and Simoni, 1989; Mitome et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction describes the role of Arg210 with supporting citations.

claim: The F1 motor comprises a ring of three heterodimers, each containing an active site at the interface of subunits α and β.
source: The F1 motor is the chemical generator in which ATP is synthesized. The motor comprises a ring of three heterodimers, each containing an active site at the interface of subunits α and β.
evidence: The introduction describes the structure of the F1 motor.

claim: Within the F1 motor, each αβ dimer has a different conformation at any point in time and can be either empty, bound to ADP and Pi, or bound to ATP (open, half-closed, closed).
source: Within the F1 motor, each αβ dimer has a different conformation at any point in time and can be either empty, bound to ADP and Pi, or bound to ATP (open, half-closed, closed) (Abrahams et al., 1994; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: The introduction describes the catalytic mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: The peripheral stalk is constructed from subunits b and δ.
source: This coupling is mediated by the peripheral stalk that is constructed from subunits b and δ (Figure 1).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the composition of the peripheral stalk.

claim: Subunit b forms an amphipathic homodimeric coiled-coil that spans the periphery of the complex linking subunit a with subunit α.
source: Subunit b forms an amphipathic homodimeric coiled-coil that spans the periphery of the complex linking subunit a with subunit α, whereas subunit δ provides additional coupling of the C-termini of the b and α subunits (Carbajo et al., 2005; Wilkens et al., 2005).
evidence: The introduction describes the structure of subunit b with supporting citations.

claim: The bacterial F-ATPase can function in reverse, employing ATP hydrolysis to generate a proton gradient across the membrane when needed.
source: The bacterial F-ATPase can also function in reverse, employing ATP hydrolysis to generate a proton gradient across the membrane when needed (von Ballmoos et al., 2008).
evidence: The introduction states this with a supporting citation.

claim: Subunit ε changes conformation in an ATP-dependent manner to prevent rotation of the complex.
source: In vivo, subunit ε is believed to change conformation in an ATP-dependent manner to prevent rotation of the complex (Capaldi et al., 1992; Rodgers and Wilce, 2000; Yagi et al., 2007; Imamura et al., 2009) thereby conserving ATP when its concentration is low.
evidence: The introduction describes the regulatory function of subunit ε with supporting citations.

claim: The C-terminal domain of subunit ε (εCTD), when not bound to ATP, opens to an extended conformation and inserts into the αβ heterodimers.
source: This regulatory function is mediated by the C-terminal domain of subunit ε (εCTD) that, when not bound to ATP, opens to an extended conformation and inserts into the αβ heterodimers.
evidence: The introduction describes the mechanism of ε-mediated inhibition.

claim: Crystal structures of both the E. coli and Bacillus PS3 F1 motors show the εCTD intercalating into the αβ heterodimers in the autoinhibited state.
source: The crystal structures of both the E. coli and Bacillus PS3 F1 motors in this autoinhibited state show the εCTD intercalating into the αβ heterodimers (Cingolani and Duncan, 2011; Shirakihara et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites crystal structures showing this feature.

claim: The E. coli F1 crystal structure captured the motor in a half-closed, closed, open conformation.
source: However, in each structure, the F1 motor had been captured in a different conformation (E. coli – half-closed, closed, open [Cingolani and Duncan, 2011] and Bacillus PS3 – open, closed, open [Shirakihara et al., 2015]) which could either relate to inter species differences or crystal contacts and crystallization conditions.
evidence: The introduction cites the conformational state observed in the E. coli crystal structure.

claim: The Bacillus PS3 F1 crystal structure captured the motor in an open, closed, open conformation.
source: However, in each structure, the F1 motor had been captured in a different conformation (E. coli – half-closed, closed, open [Cingolani and Duncan, 2011] and Bacillus PS3 – open, closed, open [Shirakihara et al., 2015]) which could either relate to inter species differences or crystal contacts and crystallization conditions.
evidence: The introduction cites the conformational state observed in the Bacillus PS3 crystal structure.

claim: P. denitrificans F-ATPase has 38% sequence identity with E. coli F-ATPase over all subunits.
source: The crystal structure of the F-ATPase from P. denitrificans (Morales-Rios et al., 2015), that is closely related to E. coli (38% sequence identity over all subunits), shows a similar overall architecture to bovine F1Fo ATP synthase as well as to the main features of A/V ATPases.
evidence: The introduction states the sequence identity between P. denitrificans and E. coli.

claim: Three cryo-EM maps of E. coli F-ATPase in its autoinhibited state were determined to resolutions of 6.9, 7.8, and 8.5 Å.
source: Here, we present three cryo-EM maps along with molecular models of E. coli F-ATPase in its autoinhibited state, determined to resolutions of 6.9, 7.8, and 8.5 Å.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the resolutions of the three cryo-EM maps.

claim: The overall F1 motor conformation in all three reconstructions is similar to that seen in the thermophilic Bacillus PS3 F1 ATPase structure.
source: In all three reconstructions, the εCTD is in an extended conformation, stabilizing an overall F1 motor conformation similar to that seen in the thermophilic Bacillus PS3 F1 ATPase structure.
evidence: The introduction states the similarity to the Bacillus PS3 structure.

claim: Density for the peripheral stalk extends the entire length of the complex.
source: Density for the peripheral stalk extends the entire length of the complex and its coiled-coil bifurcates towards the N-terminus to enter the membrane as two separate helices that clamp the a subunit to the c ring.
evidence: The introduction describes the peripheral stalk density observed in the cryo-EM maps.

claim: The peripheral stalk coiled-coil bifurcates towards the N-terminus to enter the membrane as two separate helices that clamp the a subunit to the c ring.
source: Density for the peripheral stalk extends the entire length of the complex and its coiled-coil bifurcates towards the N-terminus to enter the membrane as two separate helices that clamp the a subunit to the c ring.
evidence: The introduction describes this structural feature observed in the cryo-EM maps.

claim: The cryo-EM maps allowed interpretation of the complete F1-delta interface, showing the three α subunit N-termini in distinct orientations.
source: Moreover, our maps allowed us to interpret the complete F1-delta interface, showing the three α subunit N-termini in distinct orientations.
evidence: The introduction states this finding from the cryo-EM analysis.

claim: Each cryo-EM map confirmed the c-ring stoichiometry to be decameric.
source: Each map also confirmed the c-ring stoichiometry to be decameric, which to date has been only characterized by crosslinking and single molecule analyses.
evidence: The introduction states that the cryo-EM maps confirmed the c-ring stoichiometry.

claim: Bacterial ATP synthase is seen as an important antimicrobial target in organisms related to E. coli such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: These models provide crucial structural information on a key complex that extends our understanding of the mechanism of rotary ATPases in general, together with information on the bacterial ATP synthase, which is seen as an important antimicrobial target in organisms related to E. coli such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Ahmad et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction states this with a supporting citation.

claim: Cysteine-free E. coli F-ATPase had all 10 cysteines replaced with alanines and a His-tag introduced on the β subunit.
source: Cysteine-free E. coli F-ATPase, as described in Ishmukhametov et al. (2005) where all 10 cysteines were replaced with alanines and a His-tag introduced on the β subunit, was solubilized in digitonin detergent and purified as described in the Materials and methods.
evidence: The results section describes the protein construct used with a citation.

claim: The purified cysteine-free E. coli F-ATPase is capable of ATP hydrolysis-driven proton pumping upon reconstitution into proteoliposomes.
source: This procedure provided pure protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) capable of ATP hydrolysis-driven proton pumping upon reconstitution into proteoliposomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section states this functional property with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: DCCD at 50 µM completely abolished proton pumping by the E. coli F-ATPase.
source: N,N`-dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCCD), a compound which selectively modifies Asp61 of subunit c at 50 µM (Pogoryelov et al., 2010) completely abolished proton pumping (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and inhibited 90% of ATPase activity of isolated protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The results section states this with reference to figure data and a citation.

claim: DCCD at 50 µM inhibited 90% of ATPase activity of isolated E. coli F-ATPase.
source: N,N`-dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCCD), a compound which selectively modifies Asp61 of subunit c at 50 µM (Pogoryelov et al., 2010) completely abolished proton pumping (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and inhibited 90% of ATPase activity of isolated protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The results section states this with reference to figure data.

claim: DCCD inhibition of ATPase activity indicates coupling between the F1 and Fo motors.
source: Such inhibition indicates coupling between the F1 and Fo motors (Cook et al., 2003; Peskova and Nakamoto, 2000; Tsunoda et al., 2000).
evidence: The results section states this interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: 395,140 particles were picked from the cryo-EM data, of which 216,711 were used in refinement.
source: 395,140 particles were picked, of which 216,711 were used in refinement.
evidence: The results section explicitly states the number of particles used in the analysis.

claim: Three different conformations of the E. coli F-ATPase complex were identified using 3D classification in RELION.
source: Three different conformations of the complex were identified using 3D classification in RELION (Scheres, 2012).
evidence: The results section states the method used to identify the three conformations.

claim: In the three conformations, the central stalk was progressively rotated 120° relative to the peripheral stalk.
source: In these three conformations, the central stalk was progressively rotated 120° relative to the peripheral stalk.
evidence: The results section describes the rotational relationship between the three states.

claim: The overall architecture of E. coli F-ATPase is similar to that of F-ATPase from P. denitrificans and F1Fo ATP synthases from Bos Taurus, Yarrowia lipolytica and Polytomella.
source: Thus, although its overall architecture was similar to that of F-ATPase from P. denitrificans (Morales-Rios et al., 2015) and F1Fo ATP synthases from Bos Taurus (Zhou et al., 2015), Yarrowia lipolytica (Hahn et al., 2016) and Polytomella (Allegretti et al., 2015), with the catalytic F1 motor attached to a proton powered membrane Fo motor and single central and peripheral stalks, differences in the individual motors and peripheral stalk were apparent.
evidence: The results section compares the E. coli structure to other ATP synthase structures with citations.

claim: E. coli F-ATPase has a simpler stator architecture, containing only seven helices in the a and b subunits rather than the eight seen in mitochondrial F-type ATP synthase.
source: Comparison with the membrane-embedded motors from other sub nanometre cryo-EM maps indicated the E. coli F-ATPase had a simpler stator architecture, containing only seven helices in the a and b subunits rather than the eight seen in mitochondrial F-type ATP synthase (Figure 2—figure supplement 8), consistent with labeling approaches (Wada et al., 1999).
evidence: The results section compares the E. coli structure to mitochondrial structures with citations.

claim: The F1 motor rocks or wobbles during the catalytic cycle.
source: A movie generated by interpolation between the three states (Video 1) indicated that the F1 motor rocks or wobbles during the catalytic cycle (Kinosita et al., 2000; Stewart et al., 2012) as previously predicted, although of course the structures described here do not represent the complex in its uninhibited active synthesizing form.
evidence: The results section describes this observation from the interpolated movie with citations to previous predictions.

claim: Two pivot points enable the peripheral stalk to accommodate eccentric movement of F1: one near the peripheral stalk/Fo interface (~bArg36) and one near the peripheral stalk/F1 interface (~bGln106).
source: Two pivot points, one near the peripheral stalk/Fo interface (~bArg36) (Welch et al., 2008) and one near the peripheral stalk/F1 interface (~bGln106), enabled the stalk to accommodate this eccentric movement of F1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: The results section identifies these pivot points with a citation and figure reference.

claim: The peripheral stalk contacted all three α subunits via their N-terminal helices asymmetrically employing three different interfaces.
source: Interestingly, the peripheral stalk contacted all three α subunits via their N-terminal helices, but did so asymmetrically employing three different interfaces with each α subunit (Figure 4).
evidence: The results section describes this structural observation with a figure reference.

claim: The binding of the peripheral stalk to three anchor points in different geometries would provide a molecular key that would result in the δ subunit binding in a single orientation across the top of the symmetrical αβ heterodimers.
source: Although the resolution of the map was insufficient to assign the precise interface, the binding of the peripheral stalk to three anchor points in different geometries would provide a molecular key that would result in the δ subunit binding in a single orientation across the top of the symmetrical αβ heterodimers.
evidence: The results section provides this interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The b subunits formed a homodimeric coiled-coil that spanned almost the entire complex (212 of 232 Å).
source: The b subunits formed a homodimeric coiled-coil that spaned almost the entire complex (212 of 232 Å) with their N-termini bifurcating just above the membrane to generate two separate helices within the membrane (Figure 3A).
evidence: The results section describes this structural feature with measurements.

claim: The b subunit N-termini bifurcate just above the membrane to generate two separate helices within the membrane.
source: The b subunits formed a homodimeric coiled-coil that spaned almost the entire complex (212 of 232 Å) with their N-termini bifurcating just above the membrane to generate two separate helices within the membrane (Figure 3A).
evidence: The results section describes this structural feature.

claim: NMR analysis of the transmembrane domain of E. coli F-ATPase b subunit showed a helical structure interrupted by a rigid 20° bend at residues 23–26.
source: Furthermore, NMR analysis of the transmembrane domain of E. coli F-ATPase b subunit (Dmitriev et al., 1999) showed a helical structure that was interrupted by a rigid 20° bend at residues 23–26 that result in a structure consistent with the b subunit bifurcation.
evidence: The results section cites NMR data that supports the observed bifurcation.

claim: All three reconstructions showed the complex in its autoinhibited state, with clear density for the εCTD extending deep into the central cavity of the F1 enzyme.
source: All three reconstructions showed the complex in its autoinhibited state, with clear density for the εCTD extending deep into the central cavity of the F1 enzyme (Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from the cryo-EM maps.

claim: Fitting of the E. coli α3β3γε crystal structure into the cryo-EM maps showed that the β1 subunit had adopted a different more open conformation.
source: Fitting of the E. coli α3β3γε crystal structure (Cingolani and Duncan, 2011) into our cryo-EM maps showed that the β1 subunit had adopted a different more open conformation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes this comparison with a citation and figure reference.

claim: In the E. coli crystal structure, the εCTD contacts more subunits in F1 (α1, α2, β1, β2 and γ) compared to the cryo-EM reconstructions, where it contacted fewer subunits (α1, α2, β2 and γ).
source: In the above crystal structure, the εCTD contacts more subunits in F1 (α1, α2, β1, β2 and γ) compared to our cryo-EM reconstructions, where it contacted fewer subunits (α1, α2, β2 and γ).
evidence: The results section compares the contacts in the crystal structure versus the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The conformation of the cryo-EM structure was more similar to that seen in the Bacillus PS3 structure, where it is proposed to be in an 'open, closed, open' conformation.
source: The conformation of our cryo-EM structure was more similar to that seen in the Bacillus PS3 structure (Shirakihara et al., 2015), where it is proposed to be in an 'open, closed, open' conformation (Figure 5).
evidence: The results section compares the cryo-EM structure to the Bacillus PS3 structure with a citation.

claim: Clear peaks were seen at the nucleotide binding pockets in a difference density map, indicating that the non-catalytic binding sites in subunit α contained nucleotide, as well as the 'closed' αβ heterodimer.
source: To ascertain the enzymatic state of the F1 motor, we generated a difference density map between the cryo-EM density and our built model. Remarkably, clear peaks were seen at the nucleotide binding pockets, indicating that the non-catalytic binding sites in subunit α contained nucleotide, as well as the 'closed' αβ heterodimer (Figure 5).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from difference density analysis.

claim: The nucleotides were modeled as ATP in the non-catalytic sites and ADP in the closed site based on known orientations from high-resolution crystal structures.
source: These were modeled as ATP and ADP respectively based on known orientations of these nucleotides from high-resolution crystal structures.
evidence: The results section describes how the nucleotides were modeled.

claim: Single particle analysis revealed highly uniform homogeneity of the protein preparation, where 100% of F1Fo molecules observed demonstrated the extended conformation of εCTD.
source: Single particle analysis revealed highly uniform homogeneity of the protein preparation, where 100% of F1Fo molecules observed demonstrated the extended conformation of εCTD.
evidence: The results section states this finding from the single particle analysis.

claim: LDAO at 0.4% concentration stimulated ATP hydrolysis by the E. coli protein approximately 13 times.
source: Prior to addition of LDAO, the hydrolysis rate was 0.75 µmol ATP/min/mg protein but surprisingly in presence of 0.4% LDAO it was stimulated ~13 times.
evidence: The results section reports this experimental observation.

claim: Such high LDAO stimulation of ATP hydrolysis by E. coli F1Fo was not described in the literature before.
source: To our best knowledge, such a high LDAO stimulation of ATP hydrolysis by E. coli F1Fo was not described in the literature before and is consistent with our single particle data.
evidence: The results section states this is a novel observation.

claim: Density in Fo defined the overall architecture of the membrane-embedded motor together with two invaginations of the detergent micelle.
source: Density in Fo defined the overall architecture of the membrane-embedded motor together with two invaginations of the detergent micelle that have previously been proposed to facilitate proton translocation (Allegretti et al., 2015; Kühlbrandt and Davies, 2016) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes the Fo density with citations to previous proposals.

claim: 10 peaks of density were clearly present when the c-ring was viewed from above, confirming the stoichiometry to be decameric.
source: While the overall density of the c-ring was relatively weak, 10 peaks of density were clearly present when viewed from above (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), confirming the stoichiometry of the c-ring to be decameric in E. coli F-ATPase (Jiang et al., 2001; Ballhausen et al., 2009; Düser et al., 2009; Ishmukhametov et al., 2010).
evidence: The results section describes this observation with citations to previous studies.

claim: Density inside the c-ring corroborates data suggesting it to be filled with phospholipids.
source: Furthermore, density inside the c-ring corroborates data suggesting it to be filled with phospholipids (Oberfeld et al., 2006).
evidence: The results section states this observation with a supporting citation.

claim: A molecular model of the a subunit was built by combining helical density from the cryo-EM maps with models from related organisms, crosslinking data, and transmembrane topography prediction.
source: By combining the helical density from the cryo-EM maps (Figure 6A), with models previously suggested for the related bovine subunit, together with crosslinking data and transmembrane topography prediction for the E. coli F-ATPase (Jiang and Fillingame, 1998; Valiyaveetil and Fillingame, 1998; Moore and Fillingame, 2008; Wada et al., 1999), it was possible to build a molecular model of the a subunit (Figure 6B).
evidence: The results section describes the modeling approach with citations.

claim: The crosslinks in subunit a mapped to two clusters, allowing a likely sequence register for the model to be proposed.
source: The crosslinks mapped to two clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), allowing a likely sequence register for the model to be proposed.
evidence: The results section describes how crosslinking data was used in modeling.

claim: The sequence register of the a subunit model is consistent with the two half channel hypothesis, placing Arg210 of subunit a adjacent to Asp61 of the c-ring.
source: This was consistent with the two half channel hypothesis, placing Arg210 of subunit a adjacent to Asp61 of the c-ring (Figure 6B).
evidence: The results section states this consistency with the mechanistic hypothesis.

claim: Density for the c subunit is clearest adjacent to Arg210 of subunit a suggesting this area to be well ordered.
source: Interestingly, density for the c subunit is clearest adjacent to Arg210 of subunit a suggesting this area to be well ordered (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from the cryo-EM density.

claim: The cryo-EM maps extended previous work by showing the structure of the complete peripheral stalk and how it is attached to both the F1 and Fo components.
source: Our reconstructions extended previous work (Wilkens and Capaldi, 1998b) by showing the structure of the complete peripheral stalk and how it is attached to both the F1 and Fo components.
evidence: The discussion states this contribution with a citation to previous work.

claim: The peripheral stalk is based on a long right-handed coiled-coil dimer, the hallmark of all rotary ATPase peripheral stalks.
source: The peripheral stalk is based on a long right-handed coiled-coil dimer, that is the hallmark of all rotary ATPase peripheral stalks (Lee et al., 2010), showed near parallel α-helices, based on an 11-residue hendecad sequence repeat, spanning the space between the Fo and F1 motors, that changed into a 15-residue quindecad sequence repeat along the F1 motor enabling it to accommodate conformational changes (Stewart and Stock, 2012; Stewart et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion describes the peripheral stalk structure with citations.

claim: The overall fold of the soluble portion of the peripheral stalk is strikingly similar to that of Thermus thermophilus A-ATPase despite low sequence identity (22%).
source: Although sequence identity is low (22%), the overall fold of the soluble portion of the peripheral stalk was strikingly similar to that of Thermus thermophilus A-ATPase (Lee et al., 2010), illustrating a strong evolutionary pressure for this fold and its function to prevent rotation between the αβ heterodimers and the a subunit while accommodating wobbling of the F1 motor.
evidence: The discussion compares the E. coli structure to the A-ATPase structure with a citation.

claim: The bifurcation of the peripheral stalk coiled-coil into two separate helices in the membrane enables the peripheral stalk to bind to the a subunit in two regions.
source: The bifurcation of the peripheral stalk coiled-coil into two separate helices in the membrane was unexpected, but this arrangement enabled the peripheral stalk to bind to the a subunit in two regions.
evidence: The discussion provides this interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: Binding to the a subunit in two regions increases the distance about the fulcrum of interaction, which may help clamp the a subunit to the c-ring and counteract rotation and pivoting relative to the rotor.
source: This in turn increased the distance about the fulcrum of interaction, which may help clamp the a subunit to the c-ring and counteract rotation and pivoting relative to the rotor.
evidence: The discussion provides this mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The cryo-EM maps indicated that the peripheral stalk is able to flex about two hinges adjacent to the F1 and Fo motors.
source: The cryo-EM maps also indicated that the peripheral stalk is able to flex about two hinges adjacent to the F1 and Fo motors, enabling it to accommodate conformational changes in the catalytic head.
evidence: The discussion describes this observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Bacterial F-ATPases employ a unique method of regulation whereby the enzyme can be autoinhibited with the integral subunit ε.
source: In addition to its fundamental importance in cell metabolism, the regulation of ATP synthase is also an attractive antibiotic discovery target for pathogenic bacteria closely related to E. coli (Ahmad et al., 2013). Bacterial F-ATPases employ a unique method of regulation whereby the enzyme can be autoinhibited with the integral subunit ε.
evidence: The discussion states this unique regulatory mechanism.

claim: No reconstruction at any stage of data processing contained density corresponding to a closed/down conformation of the εCTD.
source: No reconstruction at any stage of data processing contained density corresponding to a closed/down conformation of the εCTD, and this along with the strong stimulation of ATPase activity by LDAO, suggests that the majority of the protein to be in an autoinhibited form.
evidence: The discussion states this observation from the data processing.

claim: The strong stimulation of ATPase activity by LDAO suggests that the majority of the protein is in an autoinhibited form.
source: No reconstruction at any stage of data processing contained density corresponding to a closed/down conformation of the εCTD, and this along with the strong stimulation of ATPase activity by LDAO, suggests that the majority of the protein to be in an autoinhibited form.
evidence: The discussion provides this interpretation based on the LDAO stimulation data.

claim: The position of εCTD relative to the αβ subunits was similar to that of the mitochondrial inhibitor protein (IF1).
source: Although the position of εCTD relative to the αβ subunits was similar to that of the mitochondrial inhibitor protein (IF1), the observation that it bound to all three states was different to that seen for IF1 that is bound to a single rotational F1 state (α/βDP site proximal to the peripheral stalk) in the F1Fo ATP synthase dimer structure (Hahn et al., 2016).
evidence: The discussion compares the εCTD binding to IF1 binding with a citation.

claim: εCTD bound to all three rotational states, which is different from IF1 that is bound to a single rotational F1 state.
source: Although the position of εCTD relative to the αβ subunits was similar to that of the mitochondrial inhibitor protein (IF1), the observation that it bound to all three states was different to that seen for IF1 that is bound to a single rotational F1 state (α/βDP site proximal to the peripheral stalk) in the F1Fo ATP synthase dimer structure (Hahn et al., 2016).
evidence: The discussion compares the binding behavior of εCTD and IF1 with a citation.

claim: The cryo-EM maps resemble the 'open, closed, open' conformation as seen in the Bacillus PS3 F1 crystal structure.
source: The cryo-EM maps resembled the 'open, closed, open' conformation as seen in the Bacillus PS3 F1 crystal structure, despite different nucleotide binding positions.
evidence: The discussion compares the cryo-EM structure to the Bacillus PS3 structure.

claim: The major contacts formed by the F1 motor with the εCTD in the cryo-EM maps were similar to that of the E. coli crystal structure, except that one β subunit changed conformation substantially.
source: However, the major contacts formed by the F1 motor with the εCTD in our maps were similar to that of the E. coli crystal structure, except that one β subunit changed conformation substantially (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The discussion compares the contacts in the cryo-EM structure to the crystal structure.

claim: The cryo-EM structures likely correspond to the autoinhibited conformations in solution.
source: Because our cryo-EM study was performed in the absence of externally added nucleotide, it is likely that the structures correspond to the autoinhibited conformations in solution, and the crystal structure of the isolated E. coli F1 could instead represent a partially bound state, especially since the crystals were soaked in 1 mM AMPPNP prior to freezing (Cingolani and Duncan, 2011).
evidence: The discussion provides this interpretation with a citation.

claim: The model of subunit a placed Arg210 adjacent to the conserved carboxylate residue, Asp61, of the c subunit.
source: The model of subunit a generated from our cryo-EM maps confirmed that the Fo motor likely operates using two half channels separated by a conserved arginine that directs its rotation (Vik and Antonio, 1994; Junge et al., 1997). Importantly, in this context, our model placed Arg210, which is believed to mediate the rotation of the c-ring, adjacent to the conserved carboxylate residue, Asp61, of the c subunit that has been shown to bind protons (Vik and Antonio, 1994; Pogoryelov et al., 2010) (Figure 6b and Video 2).
evidence: The discussion describes this key feature of the model with citations.

claim: Gln252 can be substituted with Arg210 and retain ATP synthase function.
source: In addition Gln252, which can be substituted with Arg210 and retain ATP synthase function (Ishmukhametov et al., 2008; Hatch et al., 1995), is positioned on a proximal helix with a similar distance to Asp61 of subunit c (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The discussion states this with supporting citations.

claim: Mainly charged residues that have been shown to be aqueous accessible map to two channel-like areas exposed to solvent by the invagination of the detergent micelle.
source: Moreover, mainly charged residues, that have been shown to be aqueous accessible (Angevine and Fillingame, 2003; Angevine et al., 2003), map to two channel-like areas exposed to solvent by the invagination of the detergent micelle (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The discussion describes this mapping with supporting citations.

claim: Residue A217 is positioned next to the periplasmic half channel.
source: Furthermore, residue A217, which has been shown to be sensitive to arginine mutation, and therefore been suggested to be near or part of the aqueous pocket (Cain and Simoni, 1989), is positioned next to the periplasmic half channel (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The discussion describes this positioning with a supporting citation.

claim: Residues E219 and H245, which when substituted for one another result in a functional enzyme, are proximal to one another in the model.
source: Additionally. residues E219 and H245, which when substituted for one another result in a functional enzyme, are proximal to one another in our model (Cain and Simoni, 1988) (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The discussion describes this proximity with a supporting citation.

claim: The models show a new level of detail for the bacterial F-ATPase, providing a template for further experiments.
source: In summary, our models show a new level of detail for the bacterial F-ATPase, providing a template for further experiments as well as to guide future antibiotic discovery in related pathogenic bacteria.

source: In all three rotational states of the E. coli F-ATPase, the εCTD had an extended conformation, albeit with a different proportion of particles observed at each state (46%, 30% and 24%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting State one to be the lowest energy.
